agree.reason: A wary reader gets a plain, unhyped case, a low-risk $59 trial, a call with the dietitian and no contract, so starting a trial week feels reasonable, though nothing speaks directly to someone who has quit similar services before.

honest.reason: The page drops the 'will lower your A1C' claim, reports all 14 results including the flat and rising ones, and admits it doesn't track medication, but it ties the 0.6-point average to the 10 who improved when the brief doesn't say which group the average covers.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 a meal, but it never turns 37 of 88 into 'about 4 in 10 have stayed more than six months', which is the figure that matters most to a reader who quits within two months, and it leaves out the trial's per-meal cost.

right_comparison.reason: The only alternative it sketches is cooking twice a day yourself, and it never sets the service against the apps and delivery services this reader has already tried and dropped.

qualification.reason: The A1C caveats are honest but give the reader nothing to check, such as retesting at three months with their doctor, while the trial terms are concrete: order by Thursday noon, delivery Sunday, cancel any time.

objections.reason: Doubts about cost, commitment, sameness and health claims are each answered with the phone call, meal swaps, no contract and the candid A1C section, but the 'I always quit these' objection is only met indirectly through the retention number.

fit.reason: It is a sales page of roughly 400 words with clear sections, pricing and a single order button, as asked.
